summary: Updates the RTP payload formats for the EVRC codec family from RFC 3558. It adds header-free and interleaved or bundled formats for EVRC-B, and a compact bundled format for EVRC and EVRC-B.

eli5.summary: A voice codec squeezes speech into small chunks. This adds new ways to pack the chunks into internet packets, including ways with less overhead and ways that survive lost packets better.

questions: what is the compact bundled format
what is dtx silence suppression in rtp
subtitle: New ways to pack EVRC and EVRC-B voice frames into RTP packets, plus silence suppression settings.

tldr.problem: VoIP over low-bandwidth dial-up and wireless networks needs to waste as little bandwidth as possible, but RFC 3558 only had header-free packets (one frame each) or interleaved/bundled packets with a table of contents, and it did not cover the EVRC-B codec.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4788 carries EVRC-B in the existing formats, adds a compact bundled format of same-rate frames with no extra header, adds a storage format for EVRC-B, and defines optional DTX parameters and four new media subtypes.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can pick the format that suits their link, and can negotiate silence suppression through SDP. It updates RFC 3558 and was itself later updated by RFC 5188.

today: RFC 4788 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3558 and has itself been updated by RFC 5188.

sections.title: What the Update Adds
sections.content:
RFC 4788 updates the RTP payload formats for the Enhanced Variable Rate Codec (EVRC) family that were defined in RFC 3558. It defines three things: support for the header-free and interleaved/bundled packet formats for the EVRC-B codec, a new compact bundled format for EVRC and EVRC-B, and discontinuous transmission (DTX) support for both codecs.

The motivation given is that VoIP applications over low-bandwidth dial-up and wireless networks need these capabilities to use bandwidth efficiently.

The three formats differ in overhead. The interleaved/bundled format from RFC 3558 allows several frames of different rates in one packet, mode change requests and interleaving, at the cost of a table of contents (ToC). The header-free format needs no ToC because each packet holds exactly one frame, with no bundling, interleaving or mode change requests. The new compact bundled format sits between them.
sections.eli5: There were two ways to pack voice into a packet: a fancy box with a label, or one chunk per envelope. This RFC adds a third: several matching chunks in one envelope, with no label.

sections.title: The EVRC-B Codec
sections.content:
EVRC-B is an extension to EVRC developed in 3GPP2. It compresses each 20 milliseconds of 8000 Hz, 16-bit sampled speech into a frame of one of four sizes: Rate 1 (171 bits), Rate 1/2 (80 bits), Rate 1/4 (40 bits) or Rate 1/8 (16 bits). Like EVRC, it also has two zero-bit frame types, null frames and erasure frames. The use of 1/4-rate frames is the key enhancement, giving lower average data rates for a given voice quality.

Because EVRC-B frames differ from EVRC frames, the two codecs do not interoperate. At session start the sender and receiver must indicate that EVRC-B is in use, for example with MIME subtypes separate from those of EVRC.

For the interleaved/bundled and header-free formats, EVRC-B works exactly as EVRC does in RFC 3558, except that the mode change request field in the ToC MUST be interpreted according to the RATE_REDUC parameter of EVRC-B.
sections.eli5: EVRC-B is a newer way of squeezing speech that sometimes uses a smaller chunk. Old and new squeezers cannot read each other's chunks, so each side has to say which one it uses.

sections.title: The Compact Bundled Format
sections.content:
A compact bundled packet is an RTP header followed by one or more consecutive EVRC or EVRC-B data frames, all of the same rate and size, with no ToC and no other header. The frames MUST be produced by the procedure in Section 5.2 of RFC 3558.

The price of the saving is that the whole session must use a single rate. The format may carry only full-rate or half-rate frames, and the rate is determined during session setup signaling, for example through SDP. As with the header-free format, interleaving and mode change requests are not supported.
sections.eli5: It is a packet with the standard envelope and then a stack of identical-size voice chunks, with no table of contents because everyone already knows the chunk size.

sections.title: Storage Format for EVRC-B
sections.content:
EVRC-B speech can also be stored, for example as a file or e-mail attachment. The file begins with a magic number, the ASCII string #!EVRC-B\n (0x2321 0x4556 0x5243 0x2d42 0x0a). The newline is part of the magic number and MUST be included in comparisons, otherwise a prefix of the EVRC-B number could be mistaken for the EVRC one, #!EVRC\n.

Frames follow in consecutive order, each prefixed by a single ToC entry extended to one octet by setting the four most significant bits to zero. A full-rate ToC value of 4 is therefore stored as 0x04. Frames lost in transmission or not received MUST be stored as erasure frames to stay in sync with the original media.
sections.eli5: When saved to a file, the voice starts with a secret handshake word so programs know which codec it is, and every chunk gets a small tag. Missing chunks are saved as blanks to keep the timing.

sections.title: Media Types and DTX Parameters
sections.content:
Four new audio subtypes are registered, and two from RFC 3558 are updated.

  • EVRC1: EVRC in the compact bundled format.
  • EVRCB: EVRC-B in the interleaved/bundled format.
  • EVRCB0: EVRC-B in the header-free format.
  • EVRCB1: EVRC-B in the compact bundled format.
  • EVRC and EVRC0: the existing RFC 3558 subtypes, with the DTX parameters added.

DTX, also called silence suppression, saves capacity in wireless systems by not sending most silence frames. Four optional parameters control it. silencesupp (0 or 1) says whether the sender can and will use DTX, and defaults to 1. dtxmax and dtxmin (0 to 255) give the longest and shortest interval in frames between DTX updates, with defaults of 32 and 12. hangover (0 to 255) is the number of silence frames sent after speech before DTX begins, default 1, and the RFC recommends 1 or more.

Other parameters include maxptime (default 200 milliseconds, ideally a multiple of the 20 ms frame), maxinterleave (default 5) and fixedrate for the compact formats (0.5 or 1, with 1/2 rate assumed if absent). In variable-rate mode silence is sent as 1/8-rate frames; in single-rate mode it is sent in frames of the same rate as speech.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives each way of packing its own name tag. It also adds settings for how often to send a quiet noise sample while nobody speaks, so the line does not carry empty chatter.

sections.title: SDP Mapping and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
The media type parameters map into the Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566). The type audio goes in the m= line, the subtype in a=rtpmap, ptime and maxptime in their own attributes, and the remaining parameters in a=fmtp as name=value.

All SDP parameters in this format are declarative, so the normal offer/answer usage of RFC 3264 SHOULD be followed. Three extra rules apply to DTX. A missing DTX parameter takes its default. If silencesupp is 0 in either the offer or the answer, other DTX parameters SHOULD be ignored. And dtxmax SHOULD never be smaller than dtxmin; if it is, the RTP sender MUST ignore the values and fall back on the defaults.
sections.eli5: Both sides list their settings when they call each other. If one side says no silence tricks, the other ignores the silence settings. If the numbers make no sense, they use the usual ones.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
The new DTX parameters are receiver options added to the existing EVRC and EVRC0 subtypes. Existing RFC 3558 implementations will not send them and will ignore them if received, and the adaptive DTX behavior of DTX-capable EVRC codecs keeps them interoperable with codecs that do not use DTX.

On security, the payload is subject to the considerations of RFC 3558, RFC 3550 and any suitable profile such as RFC 3551. It specifies no different security services.
sections.eli5: Old phones simply do not know about the new settings and ignore them, so everything still works. Safety rules are the same as for the earlier voice packing.
